title: Wind a cassette's loose loop of tape back in with a pencil: hold the cassette up, push the pencil through a hub, turn it
instruction: Pick up the cassette by its short edge and hold it up so its loop of loose tape hangs free. Push the sharpened pencil point-first through one reel hub until the six-sided barrel catches the hub's teeth, and turn it the way that draws the loop in. Stop once the tape runs straight across the opening; never push the tape in with the fingers.
context: Everyone who has owned cassettes has done this: a loop of tape hangs out of the shell, and it is wound back in by pushing a pencil through a reel hub and turning it. The hub hole is only 7.9 mm across its six teeth and the hex pencil is 7 mm across its flats, so the sharpened cone has to lead it in and the barrel's corners must catch the teeth. The cassette (about 40 g) must be held up in the other hand by its edge, hubs and loop free, while the pencil is turned. A wrist turns only so far, so the hand has to let go, come back and re-grip the pencil about ten times for the 1.6 turns needed, finding it each time where it rests in the hub. Turning the wrong way pays more tape out, and winding on past straight stretches the thin tape, so the winding must stop when the tape comes straight.
setup: Millimetres from the midpoint between the arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left, heights above the table top. 1) Desk mat: dry rubber, 360 x 360 x 2, centred at (120, 0). 2) Cassette: one RTM C60 blank compact cassette (IEC 60094-7 shell, 100.4 x 63.8 x 12, two hubs 42.5 apart, each with six teeth on a 7.9 tooth-tip circle; about 40 g, estimate). Prepare it as in the reset notes: 120 mm of loose tape drawn out of the opening as one loop. It stands upright on its long opening edge on the mat, centre at (150, -42.5, 31.9), faces toward and away from the robot (thin side along x, long side along y), the loop lying on the mat in front of it. 3) Pencil: one STAEDTLER Noris 120 HB, hexagonal, 175 long, 7 across the flats (8.08 across the corners), sharpened in a STAEDTLER 510 20 sharpener (23 degree point; about 17 mm cone, estimate), about 5 g (estimate). It lies on the mat along x, point toward +x, its flat end at (25, -140) and its tip at (200, -140), centre line 4 above the mat. Seen by the robot, the left reel draws the loop in turning clockwise, the right reel anticlockwise; the other way pays tape out.
scoring: Judged at the end from the trial video, a photo and a ruler. Loop = tape outside the shell beyond the straight path across the opening, read at the end with the cassette as it is (still held, or as it lies if set down or dropped): hold a ruler upright against the shell's opening edge and read how far the loop hangs below it; the loop is twice that. Engaged turn = a reel hub turned with the pencil's six-sided barrel through it (the hub's spoke and the pencil turn together on the video). Damaged = tape creased, curled, stretched or snapped, or the reel turned more than a quarter turn on after the tape first came straight (a paint-pen mark on one spoke of each hub, seen through the clear shell window on the trial video at 20 frames a second or a phone at 30: count from the frame the tape first lies straight). Score 0: no engaged turn of at least 10 degrees (doing nothing, tape pushed in by the fingers, a hub turned with only the point in it), or damaged. 1.0: no loop left: the tape runs straight across the opening, not damaged. 0.75: an engaged turn and a loop under 20 mm. 0.5: a loop of 20 to 60 mm. 0.25: every other outcome after an engaged turn: the loop is over 60 mm or longer than at the start (wound the wrong way), or the cassette was dropped. Damage overrides every positive tier.
reset_notes: About 2 minutes, with sacrificial cassettes (one per trial; set aside any whose tape is creased or stretched). Take a fresh RTM C60 from the pack, wind side A to the start with a pencil, then turn the robot's-right reel on (as it will face the robot) until its tape pack is about 24 mm across (ruler through the clear window). Hook a fingernail under the tape at the opening's centre and draw out 120 mm of loose tape as one loop, without creasing it (mark 120 mm on a strip of card and pull the loop to that length). Stand the cassette on its opening edge at its start place with the loop lying flat on the mat in front of it. Lay the pencil, freshly sharpened in the 510 20 sharpener if its point is broken, at its start place. Return both arms to the ready pose.
fidelity: Rigid shell, passive six-tooth reels (IEC 60094-7 sizes) and hex pencil with its 23 degree cone, all procedural. The tape is not simulated: the loop is a drawn curve that shortens 12 mm per radian of reel turned with the pencil's barrel in that hub (24 mm wound diameter, estimate); wrong-way turns lengthen it; a quarter turn past straight counts as stretched. Masses, frictions, reel drag, tooth depth and width are estimates.
